passage:
The common law of contract has long recognized that a party may be excused from performance when an unforeseen event makes that performance impossible or commercially impracticable. Courts applying this doctrine, however, have construed it narrowly. The classic formulation requires that the supervening event be one that the parties did not anticipate at the time of contracting, that it make performance objectively impossible rather than merely more expensive, and that the party seeking excuse not have assumed the risk of its occurrence. Courts have been especially reluctant to grant relief when price increases or market fluctuations are at issue, reasoning that such risks are precisely the kind that sophisticated commercial parties bargain to allocate. A seller who contracts at a fixed price implicitly accepts the risk that input costs may rise; a buyer who contracts for future delivery implicitly accepts the risk that the market price may fall. Only a truly catastrophic dislocation—war, embargo, or natural disaster—has historically satisfied the threshold of impracticability.

The result is a doctrine that prizes certainty and the finality of bargains over equitable adjustment. Proponents argue that this strictness actually serves both parties ex ante: knowing that courts will not rewrite deals, parties are incentivized to draft explicit force-majeure clauses and to price in foreseeable contingencies at the outset. Critics counter that rigid enforcement can produce outcomes that no reasonable party would have chosen, effectively punishing one side for the occurrence of events genuinely outside any party's control.
comparativeBPassage:
A widely held view in contract scholarship treats commercial impracticability as a narrow escape hatch—one that courts should open only when performance becomes physically impossible or something approaching it. That view underestimates the doctrine's potential as an instrument of efficient risk allocation.

Economic analysis suggests that courts should ask not merely whether an event was foreseeable but whether the party seeking excuse was the superior risk-bearer with respect to that event. A party is the superior risk-bearer when it can absorb or diversify the relevant risk at lower cost than the other party. A large commodity trader, for instance, can hedge against price swings in ways that a small manufacturer cannot. If impracticability doctrine were applied with this framework in mind, it would excuse performance not only when events are unforeseeable but also when the loss-bearing party is the clearly inferior risk-bearer—even if the event itself was within the general contemplation of both parties at contract formation.

Critics of this approach worry that such a standard introduces too much uncertainty: courts would become commercial arbiters rewriting deals after the fact. Yet contract law already tolerates open-ended standards—good faith, unconscionability, reasonableness—without descending into chaos. A well-calibrated impracticability doctrine, sensitive to relative risk-bearing capacity, would not destabilize commercial expectations; it would, rather, align legal outcomes more closely with what economically rational parties would have agreed to had they fully negotiated the contingency.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most directly addressed by both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Under what conditions should courts excuse a contracting party from performance?

choices.label: B
choices.text: How should courts identify which party drafted a force-majeure clause?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What remedies are available when both parties are at fault for nonperformance?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether contract law should be harmonized across common-law jurisdictions

choices.label: E
choices.text: How courts measure the financial losses attributable to supervening events

explanations.correct: Passage A describes the conditions courts have historically required for impracticability excuse; passage B argues for a modified standard that would expand those conditions. Both passages centrally address when excuse should be available.
explanations.A: Correct. Both passages debate the criteria for excuse from contractual performance.
explanations.B: Neither passage discusses drafting attribution or authorship of force-majeure clauses.
explanations.C: Mutual fault is not addressed in either passage.
explanations.E: Damage measurement is not the focus of either passage.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether courts have historically construed the impracticability doctrine narrowly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether a seller who contracts at a fixed price accepts some risk of rising input costs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether foreseeability alone should be the primary criterion for denying an impracticability excuse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether war or natural disaster can ever constitute a supervening event justifying excuse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether sophisticated commercial parties ever include force-majeure clauses in their contracts

explanations.correct: Passage A endorses foreseeability as the threshold criterion—if the risk was foreseeable, no excuse. Passage B explicitly argues that foreseeability alone is insufficient and that relative risk-bearing capacity should also govern, even for foreseeable events. This is the core disagreement.
explanations.A: Both passages acknowledge that courts have construed the doctrine narrowly; there is no disagreement on this point.
explanations.B: Passage A asserts this; passage B does not dispute it, focusing instead on how the doctrine should be reformed.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the central point of contention between the two authors.
explanations.D: Passage A cites these as paradigmatic cases for excuse; passage B does not dispute that they would qualify.
explanations.E: Passage A mentions force-majeure clauses approvingly; passage B does not contest their use.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as a reason to revise the impracticability doctrine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts have historically required that the supervening event be unforeseeable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rigid enforcement may punish parties for events outside their control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The party seeking excuse may be the inferior risk-bearer relative to the other party.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Force-majeure clauses allow parties to allocate foreseeable contingencies at the outset.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts already apply open-ended standards such as good faith and unconscionability.

explanations.correct: The concept of 'inferior risk-bearer' as a basis for expanding excuse is introduced and developed exclusively in passage B. Passage A does not raise relative risk-bearing capacity at all.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly states the foreseeability requirement; it is not unique to passage B.
explanations.B: Passage A's critics make this point in its final sentence; it appears in both passages.
explanations.C: Correct. Superior/inferior risk-bearer analysis is passage B's unique contribution to the argument.
explanations.D: Force-majeure clauses are mentioned in passage A, not passage B.
explanations.E: The reference to good faith, unconscionability, and reasonableness appears only in passage B but as a counterargument to uncertainty objections, not a reason to revise the doctrine per se—however, this detail is unique to passage B. Despite being a closer call, C remains the clearest answer because it names passage B's affirmative reform rationale.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage A that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should excuse performance whenever market fluctuations make a contract significantly less profitable for the seller.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fixed-price contract implicitly allocates the risk of price increases to the seller.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Force-majeure clauses are unnecessary because courts adequately protect parties through impracticability doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The impracticability doctrine should be expanded to cover any event that neither party anticipated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commercial parties benefit from impracticability relief whenever performance becomes more expensive than anticipated.

explanations.correct: Passage A states explicitly: 'A seller who contracts at a fixed price implicitly accepts the risk that input costs may rise.' Choice B paraphrases this directly and accurately.
explanations.A: Passage A rejects relief for market fluctuations, stating that such risks are precisely what sophisticated parties bargain to allocate. This choice inverts the passage's position.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a direct paraphrase of language in passage A's first paragraph.
explanations.C: Passage A endorses force-majeure clauses as the appropriate vehicle for allocating foreseeable risks, implying they are not unnecessary.
explanations.D: Passage A supports the narrow traditional doctrine; expanding it to cover all unanticipated events contradicts its stance.
explanations.E: Passage A specifically says courts deny relief when performance merely becomes more expensive; this choice contradicts that.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B mentions good faith, unconscionability, and reasonableness primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that contract law frequently borrows concepts from tort law

choices.label: B
choices.text: show that open-ended standards already operate in contract law without undermining commercial certainty

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that impracticability should be merged with the unconscionability doctrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that courts have historically failed to apply objective standards to contract disputes

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that commercial parties prefer subjective standards to fixed rules in their negotiations

explanations.correct: The author invokes these doctrines to counter the objection that a risk-bearing-capacity standard would introduce unmanageable uncertainty. By noting that contract law already tolerates such standards 'without descending into chaos,' the author defuses the certainty objection.
explanations.A: No comparison to tort law is made; these are contract-law doctrines cited for their function within contract law.
explanations.B: Correct. The rhetorical purpose is to rebut the uncertainty objection to expanding impracticability.
explanations.C: The author does not argue for merging the doctrines; the examples are analogical, not prescriptive.
explanations.D: The passage does not characterize courts as having failed to apply objective standards; it acknowledges the existing standards are open-ended.
explanations.E: Parties' negotiating preferences are not discussed in this context.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A provides historical examples of impracticability cases, and passage B analyzes those examples using economic theory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A defends the traditional narrow impracticability doctrine, and passage B argues that doctrine should be broadened using an economic risk-bearing framework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A criticizes judicial activism in contract law, and passage B defends courts' discretion to rewrite commercial agreements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A presents the views of commercial parties, and passage B presents the views of academic scholars who disagree with them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both endorse the traditional impracticability doctrine but differ on which party should bear the burden of proof.

explanations.correct: Passage A describes and largely endorses the narrow traditional doctrine—foreseeability, objective impossibility, no risk assumption. Passage B identifies that view as inadequate and proposes an economic risk-bearing-capacity framework to expand the doctrine. This is the point/counterpoint relationship.
explanations.A: Passage A does not recount specific cases; passage B does not analyze particular examples from passage A. This misstates both passages' content.
explanations.B: Correct. This accurately captures the point/counterpoint structure: A defends the status quo; B advocates reform.
explanations.C: Passage A does not accuse courts of activism; passage B does not argue courts should 'rewrite' deals indiscriminately.
explanations.D: Neither passage is framed as representing the views of commercial parties versus scholars; both are scholarly analyses.
explanations.E: Passage B explicitly rejects the traditional narrow doctrine; they do not both endorse it.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the proposal advanced in passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proposal fails to acknowledge that economic analysis has any legitimate role in contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposal would undermine the certainty of contract enforcement by allowing courts to reassess risk allocation after the fact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposal relies on a definition of 'superior risk-bearer' that cannot be applied to large commercial transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposal would eliminate the need for force-majeure clauses, thereby harming parties who relied on them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposal incorrectly assumes that natural disasters are foreseeable by sophisticated commercial parties.

explanations.correct: Passage A's central defense of the narrow doctrine is that it prizes 'certainty and the finality of bargains' and incentivizes parties to draft explicit force-majeure clauses precisely because courts will not rewrite deals. Passage B's proposal to let courts assess relative risk-bearing capacity after the fact is exactly what passage A's proponents warn against.
explanations.A: Passage A does not deny economic analysis a role in contract law; it simply defends the traditional doctrine on different grounds.
explanations.B: Correct. This maps directly onto passage A's argument that strictness serves both parties by preserving certainty and discouraging judicial deal-rewriting.
explanations.C: Passage A does not contest the applicability of any analytical framework to large transactions; this criticism is not licensed by passage A's text.
explanations.D: Passage A values force-majeure clauses, but its concern is not that B's proposal would eliminate them; the concern is about judicial uncertainty.
explanations.E: Passage A treats natural disasters as paradigm cases for excuse, not as foreseeable events; it would not make this criticism.
